title: How We Know Without Writing
description: Dating methods, bones, genes, objects and stories, and the shifting line called prehistory

concepts.title: Where History Begins, and Why the Line Moves
concepts.contentHtml:
Prehistory usually means the human past before writing. The Scottish archaeologist Daniel Wilson said he coined the English word prehistoric for his Archaeology and Prehistoric Annals of Scotland (1851), and John Lubbock's Prehistoric Times (1865) made it standard. A generation earlier, the Danish curator Christian Jürgensen Thomsen had sorted museum objects into a Stone Age, Bronze Age and Iron Age, which gave the wordless past its first rough sequence.

The line between prehistory and history isn't a single date. Writing appeared in southern Mesopotamia around 3400 to 3200 BCE and in Egypt at about the same time. In China it came only with the Shang oracle bones around 1250 BCE, and in Mesoamerica during the first millennium BCE. Britain stays prehistoric until Roman writers describe it, and Australia until British colonization in 1788. In between lies protohistory, the term for peoples who did not write themselves but were written about by literate neighbors, usually as strangers or enemies. Some historians dislike the word "prehistory" because it implies that nonliterate people had no history, and Daniel Lord Smail has argued for a single "deep history" of humanity studied with different kinds of evidence.

The main evidence you can dig up is material culture: tools, houses, pots, ornaments, rubbish. Objects reveal technology, diet, trade and labor far better than beliefs, names or languages. Archaeologists have a slogan, "pots are not people", which warns against assuming that a shared pottery style means a shared ethnic identity. Nationalist archaeology of the early twentieth century abused that assumption.

concepts.title: Layers and Clocks: Dating the Past
concepts.contentHtml:
The first tool is stratigraphy. Deposits build up in layers, so in an undisturbed sequence the lower layers are older than those above them (the law of superposition, borrowed from geology). Excavators record every layer, pit and wall so they can put finds in relative order. Burrowing animals, later pits and floods can mix layers, which is why the context of a find matters as much as the find itself.

Radiocarbon dating, developed by Willard Libby in the late 1940s (he received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1960), measures the decay of carbon-14 in once-living material such as charcoal, bone or seeds. Carbon-14 has a half-life of about 5,730 years, so after roughly 50,000 years there's too little left to measure. Because the amount of carbon-14 in the atmosphere has varied over time, raw results have to be calibrated against tree rings and other records, and the current international curve is IntCal20. Dates are often given as "BP", before present, with the present fixed at 1950.

Other clocks date different things. Luminescence dating shows when sediment grains last saw sunlight, or when burnt flint was last heated. Uranium-series dating measures thin mineral crusts that grow over cave paintings, so it gives a minimum age for the art beneath. Argon-argon dating of volcanic ash brackets East African fossils across millions of years. Dendrochronology matches tree-ring patterns to the exact year, with continuous chronologies reaching back more than 12,000 years.

Every method has error ranges, and the best dates come from several methods agreeing. So when you see a headline "oldest" date, it's usually a minimum or a range.

concepts.title: Bodies, Genes and Memories
concepts.contentHtml:
A single skeleton can tell you a lot. Bones and teeth show age at death, height, injuries, heavy labor, childhood illness (as bands of defective tooth enamel) and diseases such as tuberculosis. Stable isotopes add more. Carbon and nitrogen ratios in bone show whether someone ate mostly plants, meat or fish. Strontium and oxygen in tooth enamel, which forms in childhood, reflect the rocks and water of the place where a person grew up. Isotopes indicate that the "Amesbury Archer", buried near Stonehenge around 2300 BCE, probably spent his childhood in central Europe, perhaps the Alps region.1

Ancient DNA transformed the field after Svante Pääbo's team published a draft Neanderthal genome in 2010, and he received a Nobel Prize in 2022. Genomes reveal migration, mixture between populations, and the sex and kinship of people buried together. DNA can survive even in cave sediments and dental plaque. Genes can't tell you about language, religion or identity, because they record ancestry only. Preservation is uneven too, since heat destroys DNA and tropical regions are under-sampled.

Oral tradition is the evidence closest to the voices of people without writing. Jan Vansina's Oral Tradition as History (1985) showed that it can be weighed critically, like documents, while warning that every retelling reshapes it. Some traditions may preserve very old events. Klamath stories of a battle between two spirits at Crater Lake in Oregon are often linked to the eruption of Mount Mazama about 7,700 years ago, and Patrick Nunn and Nicholas Reid have argued that Aboriginal Australian stories recall coastlines drowned more than 7,000 years ago. Such links are plausible but hard to prove, because we rarely know when a story took its present form.

title: The Deep Human Past
description: Our species' African origins, its spread, the cousins it met, and the oldest art

concepts.title: An African Origin
concepts.contentHtml:
All living people descend from populations that lived in Africa. The oldest fossils usually assigned to Homo sapiens come from Jebel Irhoud in Morocco. Miners first found bones there in 1961; a team led by Jean-Jacques Hublin re-excavated the site, and in 2017 heated flints from the same layers were dated by thermoluminescence to about 315,000 years ago, give or take some 34,000 years. The faces and teeth look broadly modern, but the braincases are long and low, which suggests that the rounded modern skull shape evolved later, within our species.

Other early fossils are scattered across the continent. The Omo I skull from Kibish in Ethiopia is at least about 233,000 years old, according to a 2022 re-dating of the volcanic ash above it, and the Herto skulls, also from Ethiopia, are about 160,000 years old. This spread is one reason many researchers now favor a "pan-African" model: our species took shape across a network of populations in different regions, sometimes isolated and sometimes mixing, rather than in a single cradle.

The way of life of these people is known mainly from stone tools of the Middle Stone Age, which appear by about 300,000 years ago and are built around carefully prepared cores and pointed flakes. Signs of symbolic behavior accumulate later and unevenly: shell beads and ochre pieces engraved with crosshatched lines at Blombos Cave in South Africa are about 75,000 years old. Most archaeologists now see such behavior emerging gradually and patchily across Africa rather than in a sudden revolution.

concepts.title: Out of Africa, and the Cousins We Met
concepts.contentHtml:
People of our species left Africa more than once. A jaw from Misliya Cave in Israel dates to roughly 177,000 to 194,000 years ago, and a skull fragment from Apidima in Greece has been dated to about 210,000 years ago, though that claim is disputed. These early groups seem to have left few or no living descendants. Genetic evidence indicates that nearly all the ancestry of people living outside Africa today comes from a later dispersal, roughly 70,000 to 50,000 years ago. People had reached Australia by at least about 50,000 years ago, and probably earlier.

Outside Africa they met other humans. Neanderthals lived in Europe and western Asia from roughly 400,000 until about 40,000 years ago. Their genomes show that they and modern humans interbred; two studies published in 2024 place the main period of mixing at roughly 50,000 to 43,000 years ago. As a result, people with non-African ancestry carry about 1 to 2 percent Neanderthal DNA.

Denisovans were identified in 2010 from the DNA of a finger bone found in Denisova Cave, Siberia, before anyone knew what they looked like. Their genetic legacy is largest in Papua New Guinea, Aboriginal Australia and parts of the Philippines, and a Denisovan gene variant helps Tibetans live at high altitude. Their fossils are rare: a jaw from the Tibetan Plateau was identified by its proteins in 2019, and in 2025 proteins and mitochondrial DNA from dental plaque linked the Harbin skull from northeast China, about 146,000 years old, to the Denisovans. One bone fragment from Denisova Cave belonged to a girl, nicknamed "Denny", whose mother was a Neanderthal and whose father was a Denisovan: direct proof that such meetings happened.

concepts.title: Ice Age Lives and the Oldest Images
concepts.contentHtml:
Much of this story unfolded during the last Ice Age. At the Last Glacial Maximum, about 26,000 to 19,000 years ago, ice sheets covered much of northern Europe and North America, and sea level stood roughly 120 meters lower than today. Dry land joined Siberia to Alaska (Beringia), Britain to Europe, and New Guinea to Australia. People hunted mammoth, reindeer and horse on cold grasslands, sewed fitted clothing with bone needles, and built structures from mammoth bones. Human footprints at White Sands, New Mexico, dated to about 23,000 to 21,000 years ago, suggest people were already in the Americas at the glacial peak, though some archaeologists still question the dates.

The oldest dated images come from Indonesia, not Europe, and their uranium-series dates are minimum ages. A red hand stencil in Liang Metanduno cave on Muna island, off Sulawesi, is at least about 67,800 years old (published in 2026), the oldest reliably dated rock art yet found. A painted scene of human-like figures with a pig at Leang Karampuang on Sulawesi is at least 51,200 years old, among the oldest known figurative paintings, and a life-size warty pig at Leang Tedongnge is at least 45,500 years old.

In Europe, the ivory "Lion Man" from Hohlenstein-Stadel in Germany, part human and part lion, was carved about 40,000 years ago. The lions, rhinos and horses of Chauvet Cave in France belong mostly to a phase about 37,000 to 33,500 years ago. Lascaux is traditionally dated to about 17,000 years ago, though recent radiocarbon work argues for an earlier date. What the images meant (hunting magic, trance, storytelling, teaching) is still argued over.

title: Hunter-Gatherer Worlds
description: Bands and networks, the debate over early equality, rich burials, and seasonal politics

concepts.title: Bands, Networks and Long-Distance Exchange
concepts.contentHtml:
For more than 95 percent of our species' existence, everyone lived by foraging. Archaeology shows small, shifting camps; studies of recent foragers such as the Hadza of Tanzania, the Ju/'hoansi of the Kalahari and many Aboriginal Australian peoples suggest how such a life can work. Residential bands typically held a few dozen people, moved through the year, and changed membership often. A 2011 study of 32 present-day foraging societies found that most adults in a band were not close genetic relatives, because siblings, in-laws and friends moved between camps. Each band was a node in a wider network of hundreds of people linked by marriage, ritual and exchange.

Recent foragers are not living fossils. They are modern people with long histories of their own, often pushed into deserts and forests by farmers and states. Their lives suggest hypotheses about the deep past.

Exchange reaches far back. At Olorgesailie in Kenya, around 300,000 years ago, people used obsidian from sources 25 to 50 kilometers away, and some from farther still, which implies long journeys or contact between groups. In Ice Age Europe, marine shells traveled hundreds of kilometers inland. Seasonal gatherings left traces too. At Kostenki 11 in Russia, a ring about 12 meters across built from the bones of at least 60 mammoths, roughly 25,000 years old, may mark a place where people met, stored food or held ceremonies; its purpose is still debated.

concepts.title: How Equal Were Foragers?
concepts.contentHtml:
Many recent foraging societies are egalitarian. The anthropologist James Woodburn (1982) distinguished immediate-return societies such as the Hadza, who consume what they get within days and store little, from delayed-return societies with stored food, valuable equipment and more inequality. Christopher Boehm's Hierarchy in the Forest (1999) argued that foragers maintain equality actively, through a "reverse dominance hierarchy": the group uses ridicule, gossip, desertion and, in extreme cases, killing to stop would-be bullies. Richard Lee described the Ju/'hoansi custom of "insulting the meat", in which a successful hunter's kill is publicly belittled to keep him humble.

Equality was never universal among foragers. On the Pacific Northwest Coast, salmon-storing peoples such as the Kwakwaka'wakw and Haida had hereditary nobles, commoners and slaves.

The Ice Age record also holds exceptions. At Sungir (Sunghir), east of Moscow, burials about 34,000 years old include an adult man in clothing sewn with about 3,000 mammoth-ivory beads, and two boys laid head to head with more than 10,000 beads, a belt of arctic fox teeth and spears made from straightened mammoth tusk. Making the beads took thousands of hours. Yet ancient DNA shows the buried individuals were not close relatives, and one boy had exceptionally short, bowed thigh bones. That makes Sungir hard to read as a family of inherited rank: the burials may honor unusual people or a special event. Rich Ice Age burials remain rare and scattered across vast distances and spans of time.

concepts.title: Seasons of Politics: The Graeber and Wengrow Argument
concepts.contentHtml:
In The Dawn of Everything (2021), the anthropologist David Graeber, who died in 2020 shortly after finishing it, and the archaeologist David Wengrow attacked the old ladder of social evolution in which bands give way to tribes, chiefdoms and states. Their central claim is that early people were not trapped in tiny egalitarian bands but consciously experimented with different political arrangements, sometimes switching between them with the seasons.

Their evidence starts with ethnography. Marcel Mauss and Henri Beuchat (1904 to 1905) described Inuit who lived in small family groups under a patriarch in summer, then gathered in large winter houses with shared property and festivals. Claude Lévi-Strauss reported that Nambikwara chiefs in Brazil held real authority over dry-season foraging bands but little in rainy-season villages. On the Great Plains, "buffalo police" enforced discipline during the summer communal hunt, then gave up their powers. Graeber and Wengrow suggest that Ice Age monuments and lavish burials, such as Sungir and the mammoth-bone rings, may reflect similar seasonal assemblies with temporary hierarchies. The real puzzle, they argue, is not how inequality began but how people got "stuck" in one permanent arrangement.

The critics are many. The philosopher Kwame Anthony Appiah argued that the authors bend their sources toward a hopeful picture; the historian Walter Scheidel and others said they underrate ecological, demographic and evolutionary constraints; specialists note that the seasonal examples are few, recent and hard to project onto the Ice Age. Even sympathetic readers treat the seasonal reading of Paleolithic sites as a hypothesis, not a finding.

title: The First Monuments and Farms
description: Göbekli Tepe, independent inventions of farming, its costs, and the first large villages

concepts.title: Göbekli Tepe: Monuments Before Farms
concepts.contentHtml:
On a limestone ridge near Şanlıurfa in southeastern Turkey, Göbekli Tepe was noted in a 1963 survey, but its surface slabs were taken for grave markers of a much later cemetery. Excavations led by Klaus Schmidt of the German Archaeological Institute began in 1995 and revealed round and oval enclosures ringed by T-shaped limestone pillars, the tallest over 5 meters high. Many pillars bear carved arms and hands, marking them as stylized human figures, alongside foxes, snakes, boars, scorpions and vultures. The oldest enclosures date to about 9500 BCE; smaller rectangular buildings followed until about 8000 BCE.

The builders were not yet farmers in the full sense. The animal bones come almost entirely from wild species, above all gazelle, and the plant remains are wild cereals, legumes and nuts. Yet domesticated einkorn wheat appeared in the same region within a few millennia, and genetic studies trace it to the nearby Karacadağ mountains. Schmidt called the site the world's first temple, a ritual center where mobile hunter-gatherers gathered for feasts, and summed up his view as "first came the temple, then the city".

Since Schmidt's death in 2014 that reading has shifted. The current team, led by Lee Clare, has reported rainwater cisterns and channels cut into the bedrock, domestic buildings, and very large numbers of grinding stones and other everyday tools. It now describes Göbekli Tepe as a settlement with a strong ritual role rather than a purely ceremonial site. The idea that the enclosures were deliberately buried has also been revised: much of the fill seems to come from slope slides and gradual accumulation. Nearby sites such as Karahan Tepe show that Göbekli Tepe belonged to a regional culture rather than standing alone.

concepts.title: Many Cradles, and a Costly Bargain
concepts.contentHtml:
Farming was invented independently in several regions. In the Fertile Crescent, people cultivated wild wheat, barley, lentils and peas from about 9500 BCE, but fully domesticated forms emerged slowly, over perhaps two thousand years; goats, sheep, cattle and pigs were domesticated by about 8000 BCE. In China, millet farming in the north and rice farming in the Yangtze valley were under way by about 7000 to 6000 BCE. In the New Guinea highlands, people drained wetlands at Kuk Swamp to grow taro and bananas, by about 5000 BCE and possibly earlier. In Mesoamerica, squash was domesticated about 10,000 years ago and maize was bred from the wild grass teosinte about 9,000 years ago. South America added potatoes, quinoa, manioc and llamas; eastern North America added sunflower and goosefoot; Africa added sorghum, pearl millet and African rice. The dog came first of all, domesticated from wolves by hunter-gatherers at least 15,000 years ago.

Farming did not make most people healthier. Compared with earlier hunter-gatherers, early farmers' skeletons often show shorter stature, more tooth decay, enamel defects from childhood stress, and more infectious disease spread by crowding, dirty water and close contact with animals. Bioarchaeologists add a caution, the "osteological paradox": a skeleton with lesions may belong to someone who survived illness long enough for it to mark the bone.

Farming spread anyway because it fed more people per square kilometer and allowed shorter intervals between births. Populations grew in what Jean-Pierre Bocquet-Appel called the Neolithic Demographic Transition. Ancient DNA shows that farming often traveled with farmers themselves: people with ancestry from Anatolia and the Aegean moved into Europe from about 6500 BCE, mixing with and in many regions largely replacing local hunter-gatherers.

concepts.title: Living Together: Jericho and Çatalhöyük
concepts.contentHtml:
At Jericho (Tell es-Sultan), beside a spring in the Jordan Valley, Kathleen Kenyon in the 1950s uncovered a stone tower about 8.5 meters tall with an internal staircase of 22 steps, built around 8300 to 7800 BCE. Kenyon read it as part of a town's defenses. Ofer Bar-Yosef argued in 1986 that the adjoining wall more likely held back floods and debris, and that there is no sign of warfare. In 2011 Roy Liran and Ran Barkai showed that at sunset on the summer solstice, the shadow of a nearby mountain first fell on the tower, suggesting a symbolic or communal purpose.

Çatalhöyük, on the Konya plain in central Anatolia, was occupied from about 7100 to 5950 BCE; population estimates for its peak range from a few thousand to about 8,000. Its mud-brick houses were packed wall to wall with no streets, so people walked across the roofs and climbed down ladders to get in. They buried their dead beneath the floors and decorated rooms with plastered bull horns and wall paintings. James Mellaart, who first excavated in the 1960s, saw a cult of a Mother Goddess. Ian Hodder's long project (1993 to 2017) found little sign of rulers or temples, and isotope studies suggested that men and women ate similar diets.

A 2025 ancient DNA study of more than 100 individuals added a twist. In the early phases, people buried in the same house were often related, mostly through the maternal line; later, housemates were frequently not biological kin at all. Girls received grave goods more often than boys. The authors see practices centered on female lineages lasting for centuries.

title: Memories in the Oldest Texts
description: What Sumerian king lists and flood stories remember, and what they invent

concepts.title: The Black-Headed People and Their King List
concepts.contentHtml:
The Sumerians did not call themselves Sumerians; that name comes from Akkadian šumeru. In their own language their land was ki-en-gi and its people were saĝ-gíg-ga, "the black-headed ones". The phrase meant the people of the land in general rather than a strict ethnic label: Akkadian-speaking kings such as Hammurabi used the same expression (ṣalmat qaqqadim) for their subjects. Why the heads were "black" is unknown; dark hair is the obvious guess.

Their scribes also composed a past. The Sumerian King List survives in many copies. The oldest known was made in the reign of Shulgi of Ur, in the twenty-first century BCE; the best preserved, the Weld-Blundell Prism, dates to about 1800 BCE. It presents kingship as a single office that "descended from heaven" and passed from city to city, ignoring that many of the dynasties it lists one after another ruled at the same time in rival cities. Scholars read it as political argument, probably first composed under the kings of Akkad or Ur and later updated so that the dynasty of Isin appeared as the rightful heir.

The prism opens with eight kings in five cities before a great flood, ruling a total of 241,200 years. Alulim of Eridu reigned 28,800 years; En-men-lu-ana of Bad-tibira, 43,200. Most of these figures are round multiples of 3,600, the šar, a large unit in Sumerian base-60 counting. This section is missing from the oldest copy and from the copies found at Nippur, so it was probably added later. After "the flood swept over", kingship descends again at Kish, and reigns shrink from hundreds of years toward plausible human lengths by the time of Akkad (c. 2300 BCE).

concepts.title: Floods Before History
concepts.contentHtml:
Three Mesopotamian texts tell versions of one flood story. A broken Sumerian tablet from Nippur, copied around 1600 BCE, tells how the god Enki warned Ziusudra, king of Shuruppak, of a flood the gods had decreed; after the storm Ziusudra offered sacrifice and was granted eternal life in Dilmun. The Akkadian Atrahasis epic, best preserved in a Babylonian copy of the seventeenth century BCE, explains why: humans, created to labor for the gods, made so much noise that the god Enlil sent plague, then famine, and finally the flood.

The most famous version is Tablet XI of the Epic of Gilgamesh, in which Utnapishtim of Shuruppak builds a boat, survives the flood and sends out a dove, a swallow and a raven to find land. When George Smith read this tablet from Ashurbanipal's library at Nineveh in 1872, its parallels with Noah's story in Genesis caused a sensation. Most scholars conclude that the biblical account drew on this Mesopotamian tradition.

The search for a real flood began in 1929, when Leonard Woolley found water-laid silt, roughly 3 meters thick in places, at Ur and announced it as the Flood. But flood layers at Ur, Kish and Shuruppak date to different centuries, and nearby Eridu has none. They record local river floods, common on the shifting Tigris and Euphrates, though the early third-millennium deposit at Shuruppak, the hero's city, has been linked to the story. Grander theories, such as a sudden flooding of the Black Sea around 5600 BCE proposed by William Ryan and Walter Pitman in 1997, remain disputed among geologists and have no demonstrated link to the texts. The safest reading is that recurring real floods supplied the experience, and poets and theologians shaped it.

concepts.title: Kings and Lands at the Edge of Memory
concepts.contentHtml:
Enmebaragesi of Kish, credited with a reign of 900 years and a victory over Elam, is usually cited as the earliest king on the list whose name appears in inscriptions of his own era: a stone vessel fragment reading "Mebarasi, king of Kish", written in an Early Dynastic script of roughly 2700 to 2600 BCE. Some specialists doubt that other fragments bearing the name refer to the same man, but that core attestation stands.

Gilgamesh appears as the fifth king of Uruk, "whose father was a phantom", ruling 126 years. No inscription from his lifetime has been found. His name does appear, as a god, in god lists from Fara (ancient Shuruppak) of around 2600 to 2500 BCE, and the Sumerian poem Gilgamesh and Aga has him defy Aga, son of Enmebaragesi. Many scholars therefore think a real king of Uruk, perhaps around 2700 BCE, lies behind the legend, but that remains an inference; the poems about him survive in copies made centuries later.

Places drift between fact and fiction too. Aratta, in poems about Enmerkar of Uruk, is a rich land beyond seven mountains whose craftsmen work gold, silver and lapis lazuli. It has never been found; proposals, including the Jiroft region of southeastern Iran, lie on the Iranian plateau, and some scholars suspect it is partly literary. Dilmun is the opposite case. In myth it is a pure land and Ziusudra's home after the flood, but trade records and an inscription of Sargon of Akkad mention its ships, and archaeology identifies it with Bahrain and the nearby Gulf coast, where thousands of ancient burial mounds survive.

title: Open Questions and Their Limits
description: Language origins, the Indo-European homeland, drowned lands, and contested claims

concepts.title: Language and the Indo-European Question
concepts.contentHtml:
Some questions remain genuinely open. The origin of language left no direct trace, because speech does not fossilize. The clues are indirect: a Neanderthal hyoid bone from Kebara Cave in Israel, about 60,000 years old, closely resembles ours; Neanderthals shared the modern human form of the FOXP2 gene, once oversold as a "language gene"; engraved ochre and beads show minds using symbols. Estimates for when fully modern language arose run from about 50,000 to more than 500,000 years ago, and whether it began with gesture or with vocal sound is unresolved.

A narrower question has moved. The Indo-European family, from English and Russian to Persian and Hindi, descends from one ancestral language. Marija Gimbutas (1956) and later David Anthony placed its homeland on the Pontic-Caspian steppe north of the Black Sea, with dispersal from about 4000 BCE; Colin Renfrew (1987) proposed Anatolia, with the languages carried by early farmers thousands of years earlier. In 2015 ancient DNA studies showed that people of the Corded Ware culture in central Europe, around 2500 BCE, owed roughly three-quarters of their ancestry to steppe herders related to the Yamnaya: evidence of a massive migration. Most specialists now favor the steppe, at least for the European and Indo-Iranian branches. The Anatolian branch, which includes Hittite, remains a puzzle, because Hittite-era people lack Yamnaya ancestry; a 2025 study proposes an earlier population between the Caucasus and the lower Volga as ancestral to both. Genes are not languages, so this is strong circumstantial evidence rather than proof.

Some voices stay silent. The Indus script (c. 2600 to 1900 BCE) survives on several thousand seals and tablets averaging about five signs each, with no bilingual text. It is undeciphered, and its language is unknown.

concepts.title: Doggerland and the Drowned Coasts
concepts.contentHtml:
There really are lost lands, and rising seas took them. As the ice sheets melted after about 20,000 years ago, sea level rose by roughly 120 meters, drowning the coastal plains where many Ice Age people probably lived: Beringia between Siberia and Alaska, Sundaland in Southeast Asia, the shelf joining Australia and New Guinea, and the basin of the Persian Gulf. Because coasts attract settlement, much of the record of coastal life before about 8000 BCE now lies underwater. This is a genuine gap, and archaeologists acknowledge it.

The best studied example is Doggerland, the plain that once joined Britain to continental Europe. In 1931 the trawler Colinda hauled up a lump of peat containing a barbed antler point from between the Leman and Ower banks off Norfolk; it was later radiocarbon-dated to roughly 11,900 to 11,300 BCE, late in the Ice Age. The archaeologist Bryony Coles named the land Doggerland in 1998, and seismic surveys collected by the oil industry, reanalyzed by researchers at the University of Birmingham, have since mapped its rivers, lakes and hills. Doggerland shrank as the sea rose. Around 6200 BCE the Storegga Slide, a huge underwater landslide off Norway, sent a tsunami across the North Sea; a 2020 study argues that parts of Doggerland survived it as an archipelago for some time. Britain became an island by roughly 6000 BCE, though estimates vary.

Underwater sites keep turning up. Atlit Yam, a Neolithic village off the coast of Israel dating to about 6900 to 6300 BCE, preserves houses, a well and burials. These discoveries come from patient survey, and they reveal ordinary forager and farming communities.

concepts.title: The Younger Dryas Debate and Lost-Civilization Claims
concepts.contentHtml:
The Younger Dryas was a sharp return to near-glacial cold, especially around the North Atlantic, from about 12,900 to 11,700 years ago, just before farming began in the Near East. Its usual explanation is a surge of glacial meltwater that weakened the Atlantic Ocean's heat-carrying circulation. In 2007 Richard Firestone and colleagues proposed an alternative, the Younger Dryas impact hypothesis: fragments of a comet exploded over North America and elsewhere, setting fires and triggering the cold. Supporters point to a layer at the start of the period containing tiny melted spherules, nanodiamonds and spikes of platinum.

This is a real scientific dispute, conducted in peer-reviewed journals. Critics report that the markers are not consistently found, not dated to a single moment, or explained by ordinary processes; a 2023 review led by the geoarchaeologist Vance Holliday called for the hypothesis to be rejected, and its proponents published rebuttals. Many specialists remain unconvinced.

Lost-civilization claims are a different matter, although they borrow the impact idea. Graham Hancock's books and his 2022 Netflix series Ancient Apocalypse propose that an advanced Ice Age civilization was destroyed about 12,800 years ago and that survivors taught hunter-gatherers to build places like Göbekli Tepe. Atlantis, their usual template, rests on a single source: Plato's philosophical fable in the Timaeus and Critias (c. 360 BCE). A fair test asks what such a civilization should have left behind: domesticated crops and animals with telltale genetics, mines, metal, rubbish, pollution. None has been found, while Göbekli Tepe's own tools and food remains point to local foragers.
